case_analysis.focal_point: Whether courts applying judicial estoppel to bar a bankruptcy debtor's civil claim for non-disclosure must conduct a holistic assessment of all relevant circumstances, including actual bad faith, or may presume non-inadvertence solely from the debtor's knowledge of the claim and a potential motive to conceal it.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 521 (debtor's duty to disclose assets in bankruptcy schedules); the common law doctrine of judicial estoppel as applied in federal courts; and implicitly 28 U.S.C. § 586 (United States Trustee oversight authority)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Thomas Keathley argues that the Fifth Circuit misapplied judicial estoppel by mechanically presuming bad faith from mere knowledge of the claim and a theoretical motive to conceal, without conducting the holistic, fact-specific inquiry required by New Hampshire v. Maine. Keathley contends that judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine that demands a full examination of all circumstances — including whether non-disclosure was truly inadvertent — and that automatically barring a debtor's personal injury claim based solely on non-disclosure, without genuine evidence of deliberate manipulation of the judicial process, is inconsistent with Supreme Court precedent. He further argues that the proper remedy for non-disclosure should not be forfeiture of the claim entirely, but rather reopening the bankruptcy estate so that creditors — the intended beneficiaries of disclosure requirements — can recover from the litigation proceeds.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction, Inc. argues that the Fifth Circuit correctly applied judicial estoppel because Keathley deliberately and repeatedly omitted his personal injury and workers' compensation claims from his bankruptcy schedules, only disclosing them after the defendant filed a motion for summary judgment based on that very non-disclosure. Respondent contends that this pattern of conduct — combined with Keathley's undisputed knowledge of the claims and an obvious financial motive to conceal assets from creditors — is sufficient to establish the lack of inadvertence required for judicial estoppel, and that no further holistic inquiry is necessary. Respondent further argues that permitting the claim to proceed would reward bad-faith manipulation of both the bankruptcy and civil court systems, undermining the integrity of judicial proceedings.
key_precedents: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001) — the Supreme Court's foundational case establishing the elements and equitable nature of judicial estoppel
Browning Mfg. v. Mims (In re Coastal Plains), 179 F.3d 197 (5th Cir. 1999) — Fifth Circuit precedent applying judicial estoppel to undisclosed bankruptcy assets
Reed v. City of Arlington, 650 F.3d 571 (5th Cir. 2011) (en banc) — Fifth Circuit decision addressing whether a trustee (as opposed to the debtor) may pursue an undisclosed claim
Jethroe v. Omnova Solutions, Inc., 412 F.3d 598 (5th Cir. 2005) — Fifth Circuit application of judicial estoppel in bankruptcy non-disclosure context
Love v. Tyson Foods, Inc., 677 F.3d 258 (5th Cir. 2012) — Fifth Circuit case addressing the inadvertence exception to judicial estoppel
Barger v. City of Cartersville, 348 F.3d 1289 (11th Cir. 2003) — circuit court addressing judicial estoppel and bankruptcy non-disclosure
Eubanks v. CBSK Financial Group, 385 F.3d 894 (6th Cir. 2004) — addressing inadvertence in judicial estoppel analysis
Hamilton v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Co., 270 F.3d 778 (9th Cir. 2001) — Ninth Circuit application of judicial estoppel to undisclosed bankruptcy claims

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument — that the knowledge-plus-motive framework is not a mechanical presumption but a reasonable evidentiary inference, and that permitting debtors to escape estoppel by asserting inadvertence after being caught creates perverse incentives. However, this argument proves too much: if knowledge and motive alone suffice to establish non-inadvertence, then the inadvertence exception New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly preserved becomes a dead letter, since virtually every debtor with an undisclosed claim will possess both elements. Justice Kagan correctly identifies this logical flaw — the Fifth Circuit's rule doesn't merely permit an inference of bad faith, it effectively mandates it, which is precisely what New Hampshire v. Maine's holistic framework forbids. As Chief Justice, I would assign a narrow majority opinion holding that courts must conduct a genuine fact-specific inquiry into actual intent before applying judicial estoppel, while deliberately leaving open the remedy question to avoid unnecessarily broadening the holding and to preserve the institutional legitimacy of a decision that can command a strong majority.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito's concession is significant and reflects the strongest version of the respondent's argument collapsing under scrutiny: even a justice deeply concerned with bankruptcy disclosure integrity acknowledges that New Hampshire v. Maine's language — that judicial estoppel's circumstances are 'probably not reducible to any general formulation of principle' — forecloses the Fifth Circuit's near-mechanical presumption. From my originalist and textualist perspective, the equitable doctrine of judicial estoppel has never operated as a strict-liability rule, and the Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive framework effectively creates one by rendering the inadvertence exception a nullity in virtually every bankruptcy non-disclosure case. I write separately to emphasize, consistent with Justice Alito's concern, that 'inadvertence' must not become a universal escape hatch — courts should require concrete evidentiary support for the claim of mistake, and the burden properly rests on the debtor — but the remedy of reopening the bankruptcy estate rather than forfeiting the claim better serves the creditors § 521 was designed to protect, without delivering an unearned windfall to a civil defendant wholly unrelated to the bankruptcy proceedings. The unanimity of this conference, including Justice Alito's ultimate agreement, confirms that the Fifth Circuit's approach cannot be reconciled with this Court's precedent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: After careful reflection on my colleagues' arguments, I am persuaded to increase my confidence in the petitioner's position. Justice Kagan's core logical point remains unanswerable: if knowledge plus motive suffices to defeat inadvertence as a matter of inference, then the exception New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly preserved becomes a nullity, since virtually every debtor with an undisclosed claim possesses both elements — this is not a matter of degree but of categorical logical failure in the Fifth Circuit's framework. Justice Barrett's suggestion that the proper response to my gamesmanship concern is placing the burden on the debtor to demonstrate inadvertence with concrete evidence — rather than constructing a near-irrebuttable presumption — is a workable middle path that I find genuinely persuasive and consistent with my textualist concern for maintaining meaningful legal standards. I would still write separately to emphasize that 'inadvertence' cannot become a universal escape hatch and that courts must scrutinize the evidentiary record with rigor, particularly where, as here, the amendment came only after summary judgment pressure, but the Fifth Circuit's mechanical framework cannot be squared with New Hampshire v. Maine's explicit instruction that these circumstances are 'probably not reducible to any general formulation of principle.'

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the knowledge-plus-motive framework is not a mechanical presumption but a reasonable evidentiary inference, and that permitting debtors to escape estoppel by asserting inadvertence after being caught creates perverse incentives. But this argument proves too much: if knowledge and motive alone suffice to establish non-inadvertence, then the inadvertence exception New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly preserved becomes a dead letter, since virtually every debtor with an undisclosed claim will possess both elements. The 'caught' framing also obscures the critical factual question — whether the debtor's failure to disclose was a deliberate manipulation or a genuine mistake by an unsophisticated person navigating a complex legal system, often without adequate counsel guidance. Justice Kagan correctly identifies that the proper remedy of reopening the bankruptcy estate to benefit creditors — the actual intended beneficiaries of § 521 — better serves the statutory scheme than wholesale forfeiture that delivers a windfall to a civil defendant who played no role in the bankruptcy proceedings, and this remedial consideration reinforces why the Fifth Circuit's approach cannot be squared with equitable principles.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that knowledge plus motive constitutes a reasonable evidentiary inference rather than a mechanical presumption, and that Keathley's timing (amending only after the defendant moved for summary judgment) suggests strategic rather than inadvertent omission. But this argument proves too much: the timing of correction, while relevant, is precisely the kind of circumstance that should be weighed in a holistic equitable inquiry, not treated as dispositive proof of bad faith that forecloses further examination. As I noted in my initial analysis, and as Justice Sotomayor powerfully reinforces, the Fifth Circuit's framework sweeps in virtually every debtor with a known undisclosed claim — since knowledge and financial motive are nearly universal in such cases — thereby rendering the inadvertence exception that New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly preserved into a dead letter. The proper response to Justice Alito's practical concern about perverse incentives is not to abandon equitable flexibility, but to recognize that reopening the bankruptcy estate to capture litigation proceeds for creditors — the actual statutory beneficiaries under § 521 — addresses the gamesmanship concern without the disproportionate forfeiture that serves only the civil defendant.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the knowledge-plus-motive framework is not a mechanical presumption but a reasonable evidentiary inference, and that permitting debtors to escape estoppel by asserting inadvertence after being caught creates perverse incentives. But this argument proves too much: if knowledge plus motive suffices to establish non-inadvertence as a matter of inference, then the inadvertence exception New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly preserved becomes a dead letter, since virtually every debtor with an undisclosed claim will possess both elements. The Court in New Hampshire v. Maine did not merely list factors to consider — it characterized the doctrine as 'probably not reducible to any general formulation of principle,' language that affirmatively forecloses the Fifth Circuit's approach of treating two factors as effectively dispositive. Justice Alito's concern about perverse incentives is legitimate but better addressed through the remedy of reopening the bankruptcy estate, as Justices Kagan and Jackson correctly note, rather than through claim forfeiture that delivers a windfall to a civil defendant wholly unrelated to the bankruptcy proceedings and harms the very creditors § 521 was designed to protect.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito's partial concession in round 2 is significant — even the justice most sympathetic to the respondent's position acknowledges that New Hampshire v. Maine's language forecloses the mechanical presumption the Fifth Circuit employed. His remaining concern about 'inadvertence' becoming a universal escape hatch is legitimate, but as I noted in my prior reasoning and as Justice Barrett correctly frames it, the proper response is placing a meaningful evidentiary burden on the debtor to demonstrate inadvertence with concrete evidence — not constructing a near-irrebuttable presumption that collapses the equitable inquiry into two factors. The unanimity of my colleagues on the core legal question reinforces my confidence that the Fifth Circuit's framework cannot be reconciled with New Hampshire v. Maine's explicit instruction that courts weigh 'all relevant circumstances,' and I would join a narrow opinion on those grounds while being receptive to Justice Alito's separate emphasis that courts must scrutinize claimed inadvertence rigorously. The institutional interest in a clear, workable rule also counsels for the holistic framework — it gives lower courts meaningful guidance without the rigidity that produces unjust results in cases involving unsophisticated debtors navigating complex bankruptcy proceedings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument — that the knowledge-plus-motive framework is not a mechanical presumption but rather a reasonable evidentiary inference, and that permitting debtors to escape estoppel by asserting inadvertence after being caught creates perverse incentives. This argument has genuine force, but it ultimately fails under New Hampshire v. Maine's framework because the Court's explicit carve-out for 'inadvertence or mistake' is not satisfied by merely labeling an inference 'reasonable' — the equitable inquiry demands that courts actually examine the full evidentiary record, including debtor sophistication, counsel involvement, and promptness of amendment, before concluding bad faith exists. Justice Alito's concern about strategic gamesmanship is better addressed by placing the burden on the debtor to demonstrate inadvertence with concrete evidence rather than by constructing a near-irrebuttable presumption that, as Justice Kagan correctly observes, sweeps in virtually every debtor with an undisclosed known claim. Furthermore, the remedy concern reinforces my position: if the goal is protecting creditors and deterring manipulation, reopening the estate accomplishes both without the disproportionate forfeiture that serves only the civil defendant — a result that no equitable principle can justify.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the knowledge-plus-motive framework is not a mechanical presumption but a reasonable evidentiary inference, and that permitting debtors to escape estoppel by asserting inadvertence after being caught creates perverse incentives. But this argument proves too much: if knowledge plus motive suffices to establish non-inadvertence, then the inadvertence exception New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly preserved becomes functionally dead, because virtually every debtor with an undisclosed claim will possess both elements. Justice Kagan correctly identifies this logical flaw — the exception cannot survive if the inference that defeats it is available in nearly every case. Moreover, Justice Alito's concern about strategic gamesmanship is better addressed through the remedy of reopening the bankruptcy estate, which actually protects creditors rather than delivering a windfall to a civil defendant who had no role in the bankruptcy proceedings and whose interests are entirely orthogonal to the disclosure requirements of § 521. My background representing clients who navigate complex legal systems without full understanding reinforces my conviction that the Fifth Circuit's approach disproportionately harms unsophisticated debtors who make genuine mistakes, and that equitable doctrines must be applied with sensitivity to actual circumstances rather than through presumptions that function as strict liability rules.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001) establishes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine requiring courts to weigh all relevant circumstances, and the Court explicitly cautioned that the doctrine should not punish 'inadvertence or mistake.' The Fifth Circuit's mechanical presumption of bad faith from knowledge plus motive alone — without examining the debtor's sophistication, communications with counsel, promptness of amendment, or bankruptcy court findings — transforms an equitable inquiry into a rigid forfeiture rule that is inconsistent with New Hampshire v. Maine's holistic framework. As a matter of institutional minimalism, I would hold narrowly that courts must conduct a genuine fact-specific inquiry into actual intent before applying judicial estoppel, while leaving open the question of what remedy is appropriate when bad faith is actually established, thereby preserving both the integrity of bankruptcy disclosure requirements and the equitable character of the doctrine without unnecessarily disturbing the underlying precedential landscape.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I note that judicial estoppel is a common law equitable doctrine not codified in the Constitution's text, and its application must remain tethered to its historical equitable foundations rather than mechanical presumptions. New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), explicitly characterizes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine 'invoked by a court at its discretion,' which by its very nature demands a holistic, fact-specific inquiry rather than a rigid presumption of bad faith derived solely from knowledge and motive. The Fifth Circuit's approach of mechanically presuming non-inadvertence from knowledge plus motive effectively transforms a flexible equitable doctrine into a strict liability rule, which is inconsistent with both the historical common law understanding of equity and this Court's articulation in New Hampshire v. Maine that courts must examine the totality of circumstances. Furthermore, 11 U.S.C. § 521 establishes the disclosure duty, but the appropriate remedy for its violation should serve the statute's actual beneficiaries — creditors — rather than functioning as a windfall to civil defendants, suggesting the bankruptcy estate's reopening is the more textually and equitably sound remedy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: While New Hampshire v. Maine establishes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine requiring consideration of relevant factors, the Fifth Circuit's application here is defensible on textualist and practical grounds. Keathley had an unambiguous statutory duty under 11 U.S.C. § 521 to disclose all assets, including contingent claims, and his repeated failure to do so — only correcting the record after the defendant moved for summary judgment on precisely that basis — demonstrates the kind of deliberate manipulation that judicial estoppel targets. The knowledge-plus-motive framework is not a mechanical presumption divorced from equitable inquiry but rather a reasonable evidentiary inference that courts may draw from established facts; requiring courts to conduct an open-ended 'holistic' inquiry beyond these concrete indicia would undermine the integrity of the bankruptcy disclosure system and reward strategic gamesmanship. From a practical standpoint, permitting debtors to escape judicial estoppel merely by asserting inadvertence after being caught would create perverse incentives that harm creditors and undermine the orderly administration of bankruptcy estates.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), established judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine requiring a holistic, fact-specific inquiry, and the Fifth Circuit's mechanical presumption of bad faith from knowledge plus motive alone fundamentally distorts that framework by rendering the inadvertence exception virtually meaningless. The Fifth Circuit's 'rigid' and 'unforgiving' rule, as described in the record, ignores critical real-world circumstances — the debtor's sophistication, whether counsel was informed, whether amendments were promptly filed, and whether the bankruptcy court itself found bad faith — all of which bear directly on whether non-disclosure was a deliberate manipulation of judicial proceedings or an honest mistake. As an equitable doctrine, judicial estoppel must be applied with sensitivity to actual circumstances rather than through a presumption that, by definition, sweeps in nearly every bankruptcy debtor who fails to disclose a known claim, disproportionately harming unsophisticated and vulnerable debtors who most need access to the courts. Furthermore, the more proportionate remedy of reopening the bankruptcy estate to allow creditors to recover from litigation proceeds better serves the underlying purposes of 11 U.S.C. § 521 without the draconian forfeiture of a legitimate personal injury claim.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine squarely establishes that judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine targeting 'deliberate' manipulation of the judicial process, explicitly carving out positions taken through 'inadvertence or mistake' — language that demands a genuine, fact-specific inquiry rather than a mechanical presumption. The Fifth Circuit's approach of inferring non-inadvertence solely from knowledge plus motive collapses the inadvertence exception entirely, since virtually every bankruptcy debtor with an undisclosed claim will possess both elements, rendering the exception meaningless and the doctrine punitive rather than equitable. As a pragmatic textualist, I am troubled by a rule that produces automatic forfeiture — a harsh remedy that harms not just the debtor but also the creditors whom § 521's disclosure requirements are designed to protect — when the proper remedy of reopening the bankruptcy estate to capture litigation proceeds for creditors is both available and more faithful to the statutory scheme. The circuit split itself confirms that the Fifth Circuit's rigid presumption departs from the holistic, totality-of-circumstances framework that the majority of circuits correctly derive from New Hampshire v. Maine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly characterized judicial estoppel as 'an equitable doctrine invoked by a court at its discretion' whose circumstances of application are 'probably not reducible to any general formulation of principle,' 532 U.S. 742, 750 (2001) — language that forecloses the mechanical, presumption-based approach the Fifth Circuit employed. As a textualist and originalist, I am bound to apply what the Court actually said in New Hampshire v. Maine, and that opinion plainly requires courts to examine the totality of relevant circumstances rather than short-circuit the inquiry by inferring bad faith from knowledge plus motive alone. The Fifth Circuit's approach effectively converts an equitable, discretionary doctrine into a rigid rule of forfeiture — precisely the kind of formulaic judicial lawmaking that distorts both the common law tradition underlying judicial estoppel and the separation of powers, since Congress, not courts, should define categorical forfeitures of legal claims. Furthermore, the proper remedy concern reinforces the equitable analysis: barring the claim entirely rather than reopening the bankruptcy estate to benefit creditors — the actual intended beneficiaries of 11 U.S.C. § 521's disclosure requirements — suggests the Fifth Circuit's approach serves judicial convenience rather than the equitable principles the doctrine is meant to vindicate.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001) establishes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine requiring courts to weigh all relevant circumstances rather than apply mechanical presumptions, and the Fifth Circuit's rigid rule — presuming bad faith from knowledge plus theoretical motive alone — is fundamentally inconsistent with that equitable framework. The inadvertence inquiry demands a genuine factual assessment of the debtor's actual intent, considering factors such as whether counsel was informed, whether amendments were promptly made, and whether the bankruptcy court itself found bad faith; collapsing this inquiry into an irrebuttable presumption converts an equitable doctrine into a punitive forfeiture rule. From a practical and institutionalist standpoint, the Fifth Circuit's approach produces disproportionate consequences — extinguishing a debtor's civil claim entirely and delivering a windfall to a potentially liable defendant — that bear no rational relationship to the doctrine's core purpose of protecting judicial integrity from deliberate manipulation. The proper remedy for non-disclosure, consistent with the interests of creditors who are the actual beneficiaries of § 521's disclosure requirements, is reopening the bankruptcy estate rather than permanently barring the claim.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), establishes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine whose application demands a holistic, fact-sensitive inquiry rather than mechanical presumption — the Court explicitly cautioned that the doctrine should not punish 'inadvertence or mistake,' which necessarily requires courts to examine actual intent rather than constructing bad faith from knowledge and motive alone. The Fifth Circuit's rule, which presumes non-inadvertence whenever a debtor had knowledge of a claim and a theoretical financial motive to conceal it, collapses the inadvertence inquiry into a near-irrebuttable presumption that effectively reads the equitable exception out of the doctrine entirely — a result inconsistent with New Hampshire v. Maine's framework and the common law tradition of individualized equitable assessment. Textually, 11 U.S.C. § 521 imposes disclosure duties enforceable through bankruptcy mechanisms, but nothing in that statute or in the common law of judicial estoppel authorizes courts to substitute a rigid presumption for the genuine equitable weighing that the doctrine demands; the proper remedy for non-disclosure is reopening the estate to protect creditors, not forfeiture of the claim as a windfall to a potentially liable defendant. Methodological consistency with this Court's equitable jurisprudence requires that lower courts assess the full evidentiary record — including debtor sophistication, counsel involvement, promptness of amendment, and absence of a bad-faith finding by the bankruptcy court — before invoking the extraordinary remedy of claim forfeiture.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001) explicitly established judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine designed to prevent perversion of the judicial process, not to punish inadvertence or mistake — language that demands a holistic, fact-specific inquiry into actual intent rather than a mechanical presumption. The Fifth Circuit's approach in In re Coastal Plains and Love v. Tyson Foods creates an effectively irrebuttable presumption of bad faith from knowledge plus motive alone, which collapses the inadvertence inquiry entirely and strips courts of the equitable flexibility that New Hampshire v. Maine requires. From my perspective as someone who has seen how procedural rigidity can devastate individuals navigating complex legal systems without full understanding, the failure to consider factors like debtor sophistication, reliance on counsel, prompt amendment upon discovery, and absence of a bad-faith finding from the bankruptcy court itself is fundamentally inconsistent with equitable principles and due process. Moreover, the proper remedy for non-disclosure — reopening the bankruptcy estate to protect creditors — better serves the actual beneficiaries of 11 U.S.C. § 521's disclosure requirements than wholesale forfeiture of the debtor's claim, which punishes the wrong party and produces a windfall for a civil defendant who bears no relationship to the bankruptcy proceedings.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether courts applying judicial estoppel to bar a bankruptcy debtor's civil claim for failure to disclose that claim in bankruptcy proceedings must conduct a holistic assessment of all relevant circumstances — including actual bad faith — or may presume non-inadvertence based solely on the debtor's knowledge of the claim and a potential motive to conceal it.

case_analysis.petitioner_position: Thomas Keathley argues that the Fifth Circuit misapplied judicial estoppel by categorically barring his personal injury and workers' compensation claims without conducting the holistic, fact-specific inquiry required by New Hampshire v. Maine. He contends that judicial estoppel should not operate as an automatic bar merely because a debtor had knowledge of a claim and a theoretical motive to conceal it; rather, courts must affirmatively find deliberate bad faith and consider all surrounding circumstances, including whether the debtor ultimately disclosed the claims before final adjudication. Keathley further argues that the proper remedy — if any — should not be outright dismissal of the claim but rather referral to the bankruptcy court to administer the claim for the benefit of creditors.

Respondent frames the question as whether bad faith must be independently proven beyond knowledge and motive, or whether those two factors together are legally sufficient to support estoppel.

But this argument, while not without force, ultimately fails under my judicial methodology for two reasons: first, New Hampshire v. Maine's explicit rejection of 'inflexible prerequisites' is not merely precatory language — it reflects this Court's considered judgment that equitable doctrines must retain flexibility to avoid unjust results in edge cases, and a near-irrebuttable presumption is incompatible with that mandate regardless of its administrative convenience; second, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett both correctly observe, the remedy question is analytically distinct from the estoppel question, and even if non-disclosure is established, outright dismissal rather than referral to the bankruptcy court harms creditors — the very parties § 521(a)(1) protects — while delivering an unearned windfall to the defendant tortfeasor. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would hold only that courts must conduct a genuine holistic inquiry into actual intent before applying judicial estoppel, without prescribing the precise weight of any factor or mandating a particular outcome on remand, leaving open whether the bankruptcy court referral remedy is constitutionally required or merely the better equitable practice.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and the deliberation has only strengthened my conviction. Justice Alito's partial concession — that courts should 'at least articulate why surrounding circumstances do not rebut the knowledge-plus-motive inference' — effectively acknowledges the Fifth Circuit's categorical rule is defective, and his movement toward the Petitioner's position confirms that the strongest argument for Respondent ultimately cannot withstand scrutiny under New Hampshire v. Maine's explicit rejection of 'inflexible prerequisites.' Justice Gorsuch's separation-of-powers point resonates most deeply with my originalist methodology: equitable doctrines must remain tethered to their historical common law scope, and the Fifth Circuit's near-irrebuttable presumption represents precisely the kind of judicial innovation untethered from historical foundations that courts lack authority to create absent congressional authorization. I write separately to emphasize that the bankruptcy court's existing statutory authority under 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1) provides the textually and historically grounded mechanism for addressing non-disclosure, making outright dismissal via an expanded judicial estoppel doctrine not merely inequitable but constitutionally suspect as an exercise of judicial power beyond its traditional bounds.

Justice Barrett's textualist analysis remains the most compelling to me methodologically: the ordinary meaning of 'inadvertence' as unintentional oversight cannot be satisfied by a categorical presumption drawn from knowledge and motive alone, and New Hampshire v. Justice Kagan's point about the perverse remedy consequences — outright dismissal harming creditors rather than protecting them — further reinforces that even if the Fifth Circuit correctly identified bad faith indicators, the categorical dismissal remedy cannot be squared with the equitable purposes of the doctrine or the statutory scheme Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument — that Keathley's pattern of repeated omissions across multiple filings, followed by disclosure only after Respondent moved for summary judgment, presents compelling circumstantial evidence of calculated concealment that distinguishes this case from a simple inadvertent mistake. However, this argument actually reinforces rather than undermines the Petitioner's position: even if those facts strongly suggest bad faith, the proper response is for the district court to conduct the holistic equitable inquiry New Hampshire v. Maine requires, and his concern about administrability is best addressed through that articulation requirement rather than a categorical rule. Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument — that the Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive standard represents a reasonable, administrable inference of non-inadvertence given the practical need to deter strategic concealment, and that Keathley's pattern of repeated omissions across multiple filings makes the circumstantial evidence particularly compelling. But this argument, while not without force, ultimately fails under both textualist and equitable analysis: New Hampshire v. Maine's deliberate choice of illustrative rather than exhaustive language ('typically inform' rather than 'conclusively establish') forecloses converting any two-factor combination into a near-irrebuttable presumption, and the ordinary meaning of 'inadvertence' as unintentional oversight requires an affirmative inquiry into actual intent rather than inference from knowledge and opportunity alone. I am further persuaded by Justice Kagan's point about perverse outcomes — a rule that automatically dismisses claims delivers a windfall to defendants while leaving creditors, the intended beneficiaries of § 521(a)(1)'s disclosure regime, with nothing, which cannot be what Congress intended when it structured the bankruptcy disclosure system. Justice Thomas's observation that the bankruptcy court already possesses statutory tools to address non-disclosure reinforces that outright dismissal via judicial estoppel is a disproportionate remedy that extends the common law doctrine beyond its historically recognized scope.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that Keathley's pattern of repeated omissions across multiple filings, followed by disclosure only after the summary judgment motion, presents compelling circumstantial evidence of calculated concealment that distinguishes this case from mere inadvertence. However, as I noted in my initial reasoning and as Justice Sotomayor powerfully articulates, the Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive presumption does not merely draw a reasonable inference from these specific facts — it establishes a categorical rule that would sweep in genuinely confused, unsophisticated debtors regardless of their actual intent, which is precisely what New Hampshire v. Maine's holistic inquiry is designed to prevent. My background as a public defender makes me acutely sensitive to the reality that bankruptcy filers often lack counsel and may genuinely misunderstand their disclosure obligations, and a near-irrebuttable presumption forecloses the very inquiry needed to distinguish the strategic actor from the confused one. Furthermore, Justice Alito's own concession that lower courts should 'at least articulate why surrounding circumstances do not rebut the knowledge-plus-motive inference' effectively acknowledges that the Fifth Circuit's current formulation is insufficiently holistic — which is precisely the defect that warrants reversal and remand for a proper equitable assessment.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001) explicitly frames judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine applied at the court's discretion through a flexible, case-by-case inquiry — language fundamentally incompatible with the Fifth Circuit's categorical knowledge-plus-motive presumption. The Fifth Circuit's approach in Love v. Tyson Foods effectively converts an equitable, discretionary doctrine into a near-automatic bar, which conflicts with this Court's repeated insistence that equitable doctrines resist rigid formulations. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would hold only that courts must conduct a holistic assessment of all relevant circumstances — including evidence bearing on actual intent — before applying judicial estoppel, without mandating any particular outcome on remand or prescribing the precise weight to be given any single factor. I would further note, consistent with principles of institutional legitimacy and federalism, that the appropriate remedy upon finding non-disclosure may well be referral to the bankruptcy court rather than outright dismissal, as that approach better serves the interests of creditors and avoids converting a debtor-protection statute into a windfall for defendants.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I am skeptical of judicially-created equitable doctrines that operate as rigid, automatic bars without grounding in statutory text, but where such doctrines exist, they must be applied as historically understood. New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), explicitly declined to adopt 'inflexible prerequisites' or an 'exhaustive formula' for judicial estoppel, instead emphasizing a flexible, discretionary, equitable inquiry — and the Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive presumption effectively creates the rigid categorical rule this Court rejected. The Fifth Circuit's approach in Love v. Tyson Foods collapses the 'not inadvertent' prong into a near-irrebuttable presumption that displaces the holistic equitable analysis New Hampshire mandates, which is particularly troubling given that 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1) already provides statutory remedies for non-disclosure through the bankruptcy court, suggesting the proper remedy is referral to that court rather than outright dismissal of the underlying claim. Consistent with principles of limited federal judicial power and respect for the bankruptcy statutory scheme Congress enacted, courts should not extend a common law equitable doctrine beyond its historically recognized scope to achieve results Congress did not mandate.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: While New Hampshire v. Maine (2001) does articulate a flexible, multi-factor framework for judicial estoppel and cautions against punishing mere inadvertence, the text of that opinion does not mandate an exhaustive holistic inquiry that effectively immunizes debtors who knowingly omit assets from bankruptcy schedules. The Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive standard, as applied in Love v. Tyson Foods and In re Coastal Plains, represents a reasonable and administrable inference of non-inadvertence grounded in practical consequences: permitting debtors to strategically conceal claims from creditors and then resurrect them only when caught would undermine the integrity of 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1)'s mandatory disclosure regime and reward gamesmanship. Keathley's pattern of repeated omissions across multiple filings, followed by disclosure only after Respondent moved for summary judgment, is precisely the kind of calculated conduct that judicial estoppel exists to deter, and courts need not wait for a formal bad-faith finding when the circumstantial evidence is this compelling. That said, I acknowledge the tension with New Hampshire v. Maine's holistic language and would encourage lower courts to at least articulate why surrounding circumstances do not rebut the knowledge-plus-motive inference rather than treating it as entirely irrebuttable.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001) established judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine requiring a holistic, fact-specific inquiry — not a rigid presumption of bad faith triggered automatically by knowledge and motive. The Fifth Circuit's categorical rule, which presumes non-inadvertence whenever a debtor knew of a claim and had a theoretical financial motive to conceal it, effectively collapses the 'not inadvertent' prong into a near-irrebuttable presumption that sweeps in unsophisticated debtors who made genuine mistakes, directly contradicting New Hampshire's instruction that courts must resist applying estoppel when a prior position reflects inadvertence or mistake. From a practical standpoint, this rigid rule falls hardest on vulnerable, low-income debtors who may not understand complex bankruptcy disclosure requirements, and it produces a windfall for defendants like Buddy Ayers Construction rather than serving the doctrine's true purpose of protecting judicial integrity and creditors. Moreover, outright dismissal is a disproportionate remedy when the bankruptcy court — with its specialized oversight authority under 28 U.S.C. § 586 — could administer the claim for creditors' benefit, achieving the disclosure goals of 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1) without punishing the debtor's creditors alongside the debtor.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly frames judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine invoked at a court's discretion, emphasizing that inadvertence or honest mistake precludes its application — language that is fundamentally incompatible with a categorical presumption triggered by knowledge and motive alone. The Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive standard effectively converts a flexible equitable inquiry into a rigid rule, which contradicts the holistic, fact-specific framework New Hampshire v. Maine contemplates and which this Court has consistently associated with equitable doctrines. From a pragmatic standpoint, the Fifth Circuit's approach produces a perverse outcome: defendants like Buddy Ayers Construction receive an unearned windfall while creditors — the very parties the bankruptcy disclosure requirement is designed to protect — are left with nothing, undermining the coherent statutory purpose of 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1). The proper remedy, consistent with both equitable principles and bankruptcy administration, would be referral to the bankruptcy trustee rather than outright dismissal, ensuring the claim's value flows to creditors rather than simply evaporating.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), explicitly established judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine requiring courts to weigh all relevant circumstances — it is not a mechanical checklist permitting categorical presumptions. The Court's own language in New Hampshire makes clear that inadvertence or honest mistake precludes estoppel, and that the doctrine targets 'intentional self-contradiction' used to obtain an 'unfair advantage' — language that demands an affirmative finding of deliberate bad faith, not a mere inference drawn from knowledge plus motive. The Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive presumption effectively converts an equitable, fact-sensitive inquiry into a strict-liability rule, which is inconsistent with both the text and spirit of New Hampshire and improperly expands a common law doctrine beyond its historical boundaries — a concern that should give any court pause under separation of powers principles, as courts crafting equitable doctrines must remain tethered to their traditional scope. Furthermore, the rule of lenity and basic fairness counsel against a presumption that strips a debtor of a valid legal claim without an affirmative judicial finding of bad faith, particularly where, as here, disclosure was ultimately made before final adjudication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), explicitly declined to adopt 'inflexible prerequisites' or an 'exhaustive formula' for judicial estoppel, instead characterizing its factors as flexible guideposts to be applied at the court's equitable discretion based on the totality of circumstances. The Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive presumption effectively converts the 'not inadvertent' prong into a categorical rule that bypasses the holistic inquiry New Hampshire requires, which is inconsistent with the equitable nature of the doctrine. As an institutionalist, I am concerned that permitting a rigid two-factor presumption to substitute for genuine equitable analysis would undermine both the flexibility that equity demands and the practical workability of a doctrine that must account for the full range of human circumstances, including pro se debtors navigating complex bankruptcy proceedings. Furthermore, the appropriate remedy concern raised by Petitioner — that claims should be administered for creditors' benefit rather than simply dismissed — reflects a more equitable outcome that serves the bankruptcy system's underlying purposes under 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1) without windfall to the defendant.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine explicitly declined to establish 'inflexible prerequisites or an exhaustive formula' for judicial estoppel, instead identifying factors that 'typically inform' the analysis — language that is plainly illustrative rather than exhaustive or mechanically sufficient. The Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive presumption contravenes this framework by converting two circumstantial factors into a categorical rule that forecloses the holistic equitable inquiry the doctrine demands; as a textualist matter, the word 'inadvertence' carries its ordinary meaning of unintentional oversight, and inferring deliberate concealment solely from knowledge and motive without examining surrounding circumstances impermissibly collapses the distinction between what a party knew and what a party intended. Furthermore, New Hampshire's own application of the inadvertence inquiry — examining the party's prior briefing, opportunity, and incentive in context — demonstrates that the Court contemplated a fact-intensive assessment of actual intent, not a presumption triggered by two discrete factors. The proper remedy question further counsels against automatic dismissal, as 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1)'s disclosure regime exists to protect creditors, and barring the claim entirely may perversely harm the very creditors the bankruptcy system is designed to serve.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), explicitly established judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine that resists application when a party's prior position was based on 'inadvertence or mistake,' and the Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive presumption improperly collapses this holistic inquiry into a near-automatic bar that bypasses the actual bad faith determination the doctrine requires. As a former public defender, I am acutely aware that bankruptcy filers — often unsophisticated individuals navigating complex legal systems — may fail to disclose claims through genuine confusion or lack of legal counsel rather than deliberate fraud, and a categorical presumption of bad faith from knowledge and motive alone punishes the vulnerable while delivering an unearned windfall to defendants who caused the underlying harm. The Fifth Circuit's restrictive formulation is further undermined by the Ninth Circuit's more robust inadvertence inquiry in Ah Quin v. County of Kauai, 733 F.3d 267 (9th Cir. 2013), which better reflects the equitable foundations of the doctrine, and by the fact that Keathley ultimately disclosed the claims before final adjudication — a circumstance the lower court failed to weigh in its holistic assessment. Moreover, outright dismissal rather than referral to the bankruptcy court to administer the claim for creditors' benefit defeats the very purpose of 11 U.S.C. § 521(a)(1), which is to protect creditors, not to immunize tortfeasors.
